cim_eredeti: This Staten Island exhibit lets you talk to AI through vintage rotary phones and watch your stories transform into art
szoveg_eredeti:
STATEN ISLAND, N.Y. — For artist Stephanie Dinkins, coming home to Staten Island means more than revisiting the neighborhood where she grew up. It means inviting the community to help tell its own story — and exploring how those stories can shape the future of artificial intelligence.

Dinkins returned to her hometown Saturday for the opening of “Anchoring Home,” a major solo exhibition at the Staten Island Museum in Livingston that brings together storytelling, technology and community participation in an interactive exploration of artificial intelligence.

The Tottenville native was on hand to greet visitors and introduce an exhibition that puts AI in the public’s hands, encouraging people to share their memories, experiences, and reflections through vintage rotary telephones installed in the gallery.

Guests attend a participatory, sensory exhibition by artist Stephanie Dinkins at Snug Harbor Cultural Center & Botanical Garden in Livingston on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026.

Those stories become part of an evolving digital narrative, with artificial intelligence processing visitors’ contributions into imagery projected throughout the exhibition space.

“I’m from Tottenville, and so this is kind of a return — looking at Staten Island and who we are, what we are, what we’ve been, and the stories we have to give,” Dinkins said.

Her work explores how artificial intelligence can better reflect the cultural identities, histories and experiences of the people it serves.

“It’s like, what stories does your family tell about itself, instead of what stories the media or outside forces might tell about us?” she said. “The idea is to collect enough data to start to inform AI systems differently.”

Rather than viewing AI as a distant technology controlled by others, Dinkins said she wants visitors to become active participants in shaping it.

Through the gallery’s retrofitted telephones, visitors can share personal stories with an AI-powered application called The Stories We Tell Our Machines. The recordings are processed through a generative AI system that creates images inspired by the contributions, adding new layers to a collective visual narrative.

The installation also draws on oral histories from the Staten Island Museum’s collection, including recollections from the Black Angels of Sea View Hospital, residents of Sandy Ground and community leaders in Park Hill.

Rylee Eterginoso, the museum’s director of curatorial affairs and programs, said the exhibition is designed to change as more people contribute.

“What it looks like in six months is very different from what it looks like today,” Eterginoso said. “And so we encourage people to come and participate and contribute and gift their stories.”

The exhibition’s opening attracted visitors from beyond Staten Island, including Christina Latimer, who took the Staten Island Ferry from Manhattan with her son, Raymond Cedars, 12, and his friend, Rainer Boss-Redman, 11.

Raymond tried one of the vintage telephones, using it to interact with the AI system.

Asked what he talked about, the seventh-grader said he told it jokes.

And how did the artificial intelligence respond?

Sehee Kim of Queens also attended the opening.

Kim, who studied painting under Dinkins and had her as a thesis reader while pursuing a master’s degree in fine arts, said she sees a connection between the artist’s work with advanced technology and her own traditional artistic medium.

“It’s just different in the medium that we try to express ourselves,” Kim said. “The bottom line, it’s all about the core. And the core is like what matters.”

For Dinkins, the exhibition represents the culmination of a creative journey that began more than a decade ago. She said her interest in artificial intelligence dates to 2014, when she encountered Bina48, a socially engaged robot designed to interact with people.

Dinkins became fascinated by the possibility of creating a robot capable of communicating with emotional intelligence. But she also recognized the dangers of technology built on limited representations of people and their experiences.

That realization prompted her to investigate how AI systems could become more informed by the communities they represent.

“I think that AI systems need those kinds of stories, ideas, and data to potentially be better caretakers of the humans that they interact with all the time,” she said.

She said she hopes Anchoring Home will also encourage people who are apprehensive about artificial intelligence to engage with it rather than dismiss it.

“I hope that people will just come and soften a little bit toward AI,” Dinkins said. “It’s really important that we get to know the systems we’re thinking about.”

Dinkins grew up at the corner of Fisher Avenue and Arthur Kill Road in Tottenville. She attended PS 1, Totten Intermediate School (I.S. 34) and Tottenville High School, where she developed an early interest in photography, spending time in the school’s darkroom.

She recalled having her first significant exhibition at the Staten Island Museum around 1994 or 1995, featuring photographs from her travels in Central America.

Since then, her career has taken her to international recognition for her pioneering work at the intersection of art and artificial intelligence.

Dinkins is a Lincoln Center Collider Fellow, a Schmidt Futures AI2050 Senior Fellow and the inaugural recipient of the LG Guggenheim Award in 2023.

In 2023, she was also named to TIME magazine’s list of the 100 Most Influential People in AI.

Janice Monger, the museum’s president and CEO, said the exhibition reflects the institution’s commitment to encouraging curiosity, dialogue and shared experiences.

The exhibition also connects with the museum’s ACEGen Initiative, which promotes access, collaboration and equity in genealogy.

Monger encouraged visitors to contribute their own stories, memories and ideas, emphasizing that the installation is not a static work of art, but a collective experience that will continue to grow throughout its run.

Anchoring Home will remain on view at the Staten Island Museum through October 2027, giving visitors ample opportunity to participate and become part of its evolving narrative.
